name: Nikhil Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in business, aiming for finance. A normal week is three lectures a day, one tutorial where we do case studies, and then cricket practice on Wednesday night with the university's second team. Weekends I do shifts on the checkout at a supermarket near my halls. My dad manages a bank branch and my mum teaches primary school, so I grew up with a fairly strict timetable. I use the AI tool now and then, mainly to explain things I didn't catch in a lecture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. Most of the time new technology turns out to be a useful tool, not a revolution. At the supermarket we've got self-checkouts and they need a staff member standing next to them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be pretty settled. I want a graduate job at a bank or an insurer, and in this world those still exist. My parents help with some of the rent, and between that and the checkout I'm okay. My worry is the loan and that a bank graduate scheme gets 3,000 applications for 40 places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, keep the supermarket job and cricket, because it keeps me sane and gets me out. I'd apply for the spring insight week at a bank and start asking my dad's contacts for advice. I'd also try to save about 70 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A steady, comfortable feeling. Not exciting, but that's okay. I like a plan that doesn't get thrown up in the air.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned 3,000 applicants for 40 places. How do you feel about those odds?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I've always known it was competitive. My plan is to be reliable and well prepared and have something on my CV besides grades, which is why the checkout and cricket matter. Dad says banks hire people who turn up and are decent with customers, and I'd like to believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad's bank look like from the inside right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quieter. Two branches in the region closed last year, and more customers do things on the app. He doesn't say much, but I can tell he's watching it. He says the human side, a person who knows your name, is what keeps a local branch alive.

say: I'd say new technology usually becomes a **useful tool**, not a revolution.
I'd mention the self-checkouts still need **staff** beside them.
think: Bank graduate jobs still exist, so I feel **settled**.
The odds are 3,000 applicants for **40 places**, and I carry a loan.
do: **Keep** the supermarket shifts and Wednesday cricket.
**Apply** for a spring insight week at a bank.
**Save** 70 a month and ask my dad's contacts for advice.
feel: I like a plan that **doesn't** get thrown up in the air.
S0.quote: Banks hire people who turn up and are decent with customers, and I'd like to believe that.
fieldNote: Plans a **steady path** into banking through reliability and CV extras.
His father's branch closures give him a quiet, real view of the industry.
Calm is conditional on the graduate scheme odds, which he knows are long.

steps.text: Keep working weekend checkout shifts at the supermarket
Apply for a bank's spring insight week
Ask Dad's contacts for advice on graduate schemes
Save 70 a month from the supermarket wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a normal change, like cash machines or online banking, and people will adjust. I'd also say a bank has to remember it's a bank, which is about trust, and trust is a human thing. I'd say that to my dad at dinner and see what he says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it makes me uneasy. A first-year bank trainee does checking, planning, answering customers and booking, which is exactly the stuff the card says goes first. If banks hire half as many graduates, my 3,000-for-40 becomes 3,000-for-20.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the tool properly, rather than now and then, so I know how a bank would use it. I'd take a data module and a coding basics course online. I'd also try to get a customer-facing job at the supermarket, like the customer service desk, because I'd learn how to deal with a worried person. And I'd keep applying to everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly tense, like waiting for a cricket match to start in the rain. Will it go on? Will it be shortened? You just don't know, so you get your kit ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be using the tool properly. What changes for you in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for case studies and then check the answer myself, in a notebook, and see where it goes wrong. I'd also ask it to quiz me on finance terms. I think banks will value the people who can use the tool and still spot an error.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says the bank has seen change before and the people who stayed are the ones who learned. But he also says they've stopped replacing some of the back-office staff. He tells me to keep my options open, which from a man who has been at the same bank for 27 years is quite something.

say: I'd say it's a **normal change**, like cash machines and online banking.
I'd say a bank is about **trust**, and trust is human.
think: A bank trainee's **first-year tasks** are the ones that go first.
If hiring halves, the odds go from 3,000 for 40 to **3,000 for 20**.
do: **Use** the tool properly and check its answers in a notebook.
**Take** a data module and an online coding course.
**Try** the supermarket customer service desk for people skills.
feel: **Mildly tense**, like waiting for cricket in the rain.
I'd get my **kit ready**, not panic.
S1.quote: I think banks will value the people who can use the tool and still spot an error.
fieldNote: Steady adaptability: he moves from occasional to **proper use** and keeps checking the output.
The numbers are his lens: 3,000 applicants for 40 places could become 20.
His father's 27 years at one bank give him a sense of how change is absorbed.

steps.text: Use the AI tool daily and check its answers by hand
Take a data analysis module and an online coding course
Move to the supermarket's customer service desk
Ask Dad which back-office roles his bank stopped filling

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should all stay calm and keep going, and that the people in charge need to show they've got a plan. Two years isn't long, and I'd say it as a decent captain would, not as a doom merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be frightened. My degree is built for exactly the thinking jobs that go first. If the bank hires nobody for a few years, I'd be a graduate in 2029 with nowhere to go. And Dad's bank would be one of the first to reduce, so my parents' help could be at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for something stable and hands-on, as quickly as I could. Maybe an apprenticeship or a trade, like electrical or HVAC, where I'd be needed until the robots come in 2031 and perhaps after. I'd keep the supermarket job and cricket, because they keep my head straight. I'd talk to my parents about whether I should finish the degree at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like standing at the crease and seeing the bowler move his arm faster than I thought possible. A tight stomach, shaky hands, but you still have to take the ball.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might not finish the degree. What would make you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the bank's graduate scheme was closed for the next two years, and the career officer couldn't tell me where graduates in my course were landing. I'd probably go and speak to Dad's friend who has an electrical firm. My dad's friend says there's always a need for someone who can climb into a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmly, with numbers. I'd say what I think the degree is worth and what a trade would pay. Dad would be disappointed, I think, because he wants a banker for a son. But Mum would listen, and she'd say take your time. I'd do it over Sunday lunch, when everyone's fed.

say: I'd say we should **stay calm** and keep going.
I'd say leaders must show they have a **plan**.
think: My degree is built for the **thinking jobs** that go first.
If Dad's bank reduces, my parents' **help** could be at risk.
do: **Look** for a stable hands-on apprenticeship, such as electrical work.
**Keep** the supermarket job and cricket to stay level.
**Talk** to my parents about whether to finish the degree.
feel: **Tight stomach** and shaky hands, like facing a faster bowler.
S2.quote: My dad's friend says there's always a need for someone who can climb into a roof.
fieldNote: Moves toward a **hands-on trade** while keeping the family conversation calm and numerical.
His father's bank is both his career model and his risk.
Cricket is his language for fear and for coping.

steps.text: Ask Dad's electrician friend about an apprenticeship
Compare a trade course with finishing my degree
Keep the supermarket job and Wednesday cricket
Talk to my parents over Sunday lunch about my options

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ready, as long as people don't wait. I'd tell my friends to build skills and some savings. I'd also say employers should keep hiring juniors and not just wait for the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years takes me past graduation and into the first job. That's the awkward bit. I could end up in a world where the jobs I trained for are shrinking. But I'd have savings, a degree, and a few years' experience if I was lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and apply for a bank scheme, but I'd also apply to smaller firms, like a local building society or an accountancy, which might be slower to change. I'd learn the tool well and take a data module. I'd save about 100 a month and think about moving to a cheaper town if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A steady unease. Like a long innings where you know the bowling's going to be harder after lunch. You settle in, play it out, and watch your footwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd apply to smaller firms. Why would those be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller firms have fewer layers and still rely on people who know customers. A building society in a town like ours still has a human at the counter. They'd probably be slower to bring in machines, though not forever. It's a bet, but a better one than a big bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if you couldn't get a graduate job at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take a supermarket management scheme, honestly. Customer service and teams, which I've done. It's not what I planned, but it's a wage, and I'd keep applying to finance. I don't think there's shame in that, and my dad wouldn't either, though he'd go quiet.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if people don't wait.
I'd say employers should **keep hiring juniors**.
think: Five years takes me **past graduation** into my first job.
I might end up where my trained-for jobs are **shrinking**.
do: **Apply** to big banks and to smaller local firms.
**Take** a data module and use the tool properly.
**Save** 100 a month and consider a cheaper town.
feel: A **steady unease**, like a long innings after lunch.
I'd **settle in** and watch my footwork.
S3.quote: A building society in a town like ours still has a human at the counter.
fieldNote: Chooses **smaller, slower** employers as a calculated bet.
Accepts a supermarket management scheme as a fallback without shame.
Anxious because graduation and the change arrive together.

steps.text: Apply to local building societies as well as big banks
Take a data module and practise with the AI tool
Save 100 a month from placement wages
Price up a cheaper town if graduate jobs dry up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so be prepared but not afraid. I'd say it to my dad, who would nod and say something about his own first year in banking. I'd say a lot of this is in how you handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 28, with a decent bank career or something similar, savings and maybe a house. Ten years is enough time for me to adapt, because I've always done that gradually. I'd have the tool as a normal part of my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, join a graduate scheme, and learn the tools in my first job rather than rush now. I'd save as much as I could early. I'd also pick up a skill beyond finance, like data or project management, so I'm useful in more than one place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A calm that comes from having time. I'd keep doing the normal thing, like cricket and my shifts, and let the plan run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you adapt gradually. Is there a downside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I might be too slow if the change is quick. I'd rather be second than first, but being third is no good, so each year I'd try one new tool or skill, and put it on my CV. It's a small habit, but it keeps me moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And how does it feel for your parents in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better. Dad would retire around then, on his pension, before the worst of it. Mum's school job is safe for a good while. I'd have time to help them with the house and be someone they don't have to worry about. That's the best part of a long timeline for me.

say: I'd say a decade means be **prepared but not afraid**.
I'd say a lot depends on **how you handle it**.
think: By 2036 I'd be **28** with a career, savings and maybe a house.
Ten years suits my **gradual** way of adapting.
do: **Finish** the degree and join a graduate scheme.
**Learn** the tools in my first job, not in a rush now.
**Add** a skill beyond finance, like data or project management.
feel: I'd keep the **normal things** going and let the plan run.
S4.quote: I'd rather be second than first, but being third is no good, so each year I'd try one new tool or skill, and put it on my CV.
fieldNote: His gradual adaptability gets a **rule**: one new tool or skill per year.
A long timeline lets him imagine helping his parents, not only himself.
Reassured by his father's pension arriving before the worst.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a bank graduate scheme
Try one new tool or skill every year
Save 120 a month from my first salary
Help my parents with their house when Dad retires

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. It lands before I've finished the degree, and banks are the sort of place that would change first, which means my dad and my own plans at once. What would help is clear information early, employers still hiring trainees, and training that's linked to real jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think business students are all headed for the same sort of job. Plenty of business students come from families who are watching their own work change. I'd like to be asked what my parents see, not just what I plan.

headlineQuote: Plenty of business students come from families who are watching their own work change.
portrait: Nikhil is an **18-year-old** business student who plays cricket and works weekend checkout shifts.
He uses AI **now and then**, checks its answers and moves only once things are proven.
His **traditional** side shows in loyalty to family, steady planning and a preference for work over handouts.
His dad's bank-branch closures give him an **inside view** of how finance is changing.
He is calm in the quiet world, anxious when AGI is near, then calm again with a decade to adapt.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it hits his dad's bank and his own plans together.
whatWouldHelp: Early, clear **information** and employers who still hire trainees.
Training tied to **real jobs**, not general promises.
